Fishman absolutely eats this one up, locking into a relentless, jazz-funk groove that shakes the rafters loose. Trey channels his inner Scofield, firing off wah-drenched, angular runs that dance around Page’s clavinet stabs with razor-sharp precision. Mike keeps it nasty, snarling and popping, pushing the jam into an explosion of polyrhythmic madness. Just when it they might lose control, Fish reels it back in with a thunderous fill, slamming the door on one of filthiest funk throwdowns of tour.

Trey leans into Peter Green’s ghostly phrasing, his tone dripping with reverb and just enough bite to make each note sting. Mike and Fish hold it down with a sparse, almost hesitant groove, letting the space between notes breathe and ache. Page adds eerie, sustained organ thats creep in like distant fog, deepening the song’s haunted feel. When Trey finally lets loose, it’s not with fireworks but with slow, anguished bends that seem to bleed right into the ether—pure, unfiltered heartbreak.

Fish is the obvious MVP here, somehow yodeling, drumming, and possibly levitating all at once. Trey and Page trade rapid fire licks, nailing the song’s dizzying riffs before Trey erupts into a fuzzed-out, whammy-bar-laced shredfest. Mike's locked in but throws in just enough slippery, Jaco-esque runs to keep things from feeling too rigid. During the yodel-fueled sprint, the crowd is in full chaos mode —equal parts laughter and sheer disbelief.

As soon as those breezy, reggae-lite chords hit, I know this is my chance—I’ve been holding it in for three songs too many. I weave through the crowd, make it to the bathroom, and of course, there’s a massive line because half the venue had the same idea. The muffled sounds of Trey noodling in the background confirm I made the right choice, the jam sounding like it’s stuck on the road between Omaha and Kansas City while I do the impatient, shifting-foot dance.

Fish locks into a crisp, driving shuffle, channeling just enough of Purdy’s pocket. Trey leans into the sharp, stabbing rhythm work before cutting loose with a solo that starts clean and nimble but gradually warps into a snarling, wah-drenched attack. Page is all over this one, his Rhodes shimmering through the mix while his organ swells push the jam into full-steam-ahead mode. By the final it feels like Phish just crash-landed in Countdown to Ecstasy.

Fish’s double-time gallop fuels this rock-opera behemoth while Trey slashes power chords and soars into an arena-rock solo. Page goes full Steinman with dramatic piano flourishes, and Mike locks in like a runaway train. As the final ascent peaks, Trey wails, the crowd screams, and for a moment, this one might never land. It lands. As soon as it closes the show, I head on lot where I down my ritual post-show meal. I may be slamming a veggie burrito but my mind is on meatloaf.

Mike’s brooding bass and Fish’s ominous cymbals set the pulse as Trey weaves eerie, feedback-laced swells. Page drapes the jam in synth haze, pushing tension without release. Trey’s solo claws skyward in slow bursts, never quite resolving, leaving the crowd suspended in its haunting afterglow. I ask my show buddy wtf is this? He says I think it's a new TAB song.

Fish somehow nails Peart’s fills while keeping it loose, Mike’s bass growls, and Page’s synth waves flood the mix. Trey doesn’t mimic Lifeson but stretches the solo with whammy bends and delay. The final riff slams down, the crowd roars, and Phish tips their hat to the masters of meticulous madness and, in turn, I tip my hat to the one Rush fan in my section, who's excitement of this Phish debut both at once grating and endearing.

Page takes charge from the jump, nailing the swirling organ intro before Trey and Mike lock into that iconic, hyperactive riff. Fish lets the song breathe, riding the line between Bruford’s tight precision and his own playful swing. The jam opens into a delay-drenched spiral, with Trey stretching notes skyward while Page doubles down on the proggy theatrics. By the final chorus, half the crowd is awed and amused they pulled off Roundabout with a straight face the other half calling it Progtichor

Mike's fuzzed-out bass snarls as Trey slashes the riff with bluesy abandon. The jam veers into a slinky, clav-heavy funk vamp before Trey rips a wah-drenched solo. Just when it's getting really hot, Trey inexplicably ripcords into the Wedge.

The Farmhouse->Party Time opener beguiled us. But soon we were in on the joke for it was ain't nothin but a house party!!  Fish’s pounding backbeat and Trey’s chunky chords set the room ablaze while Page hammers out rowdy piano fills. Mike keeps things bouncing just enough to stay loose. The call-and-response chorus explodes, the crowd is fully in party mode, and the whole place might actually cave in.

Page on vocals, his delivery both reverent and playful, while his piano work absolutely soars. Fish and Mike lock into a tight, bouncing groove, giving Trey room to weave in chiming arpeggios before unleashing a mid-song solo that leans into watery, Leslie-soaked tones. The jam stretches into an almost Reba-like passage, with Page’s synths swirling around Trey’s looping, melodic flourishes before they snap back into the triumphant outro. I turn to see Diskin's shit-eating grin and mark it a 0.

Trey takes a delicate approach, his tone soaked in reverb as he gently eases into the iconic opening riff, each note hanging in the air like a ghost. Mike’s bass carries the weight of the song, thick and melodic, locking in with Fishman’s restrained, heartbeat groove. Page’s synth textures swirl beneath the surface, adding an eerie depth that builds as Trey’s solo unfolds—slow, mournful, dripping. When the band crashes into the final chorus, the crowd is locked in, lost in its desperate beauty.

Mike and Fish lock into a tight but slightly looser groove than the original, giving the song a bit more swing while still driving it forward with urgency. Trey leans into the hypnotic guitar lines, blending precision with just enough grit to make it feel alive, his tone sharp and wiry but drenched in just a hint of delay. During this shocking cover, I take a moment to look at my friends and realize that  these people I've met along the way provide all the cover I need.

Page's rather unconvincing husky vocals try to set the tone, but it's Trey’s choppy rhythms and Leslie-drenched solo that stretches the jam skyward. Fish and Mike lock into a relaxed but propulsive pocket, giving the jam an almost Weight-like lope before it lifts off into a swirling, delay-heavy climax. In the much anticipated final stanzas, an obnoxious segment of the crowd “WOOOOs" along much to the chagrin of longtime fans sadly returning me from space, captain.
